title: Upward motion and measuring g
prior_knowledge_summary: Gravitational acceleration g is constant and downward near Earth's surface when air resistance is negligible.
A consistent vertical sign convention controls the signs of u, v, a and s.
The three registered constant-acceleration equations can solve free-fall problems.
new_learning: An upward-moving object still has downward acceleration.
At maximum height, instantaneous velocity is zero but acceleration is still downward g.
Upward launch can be split into ascent and descent stages with a shared turning point.
A falling-object experiment can determine g from measured distance and time or from a linear graph.
not_yet_taught: Uncertainty calculations beyond identifying limitations and improvements
learning_outcomes: Calculate time and maximum height for an upward launch.
Link ascent and descent stages using the turning point.
Describe a falling-object experiment for g, including measurement, processing, repetition and limitations.
knowledge_boundary: Vertical motion only. Experimental processing uses s = 1/2 gt^2 for release from rest. Projectile components and formal uncertainty calculations are excluded.

visual_rules.reason: Six varied visuals distribute teaching across the launch sequence, sign model, graph meaning, worked reasoning, apparatus and synthesis.

evidence_basis.evidence_gap: No mapped P2 part covers the falling-object experiment; experimental questions are grounded only in controlled syllabus outcome 9702_t02_m01_o08.
evidence_basis.canonical_audit: Checked canonical questions, mark schemes, the launch-path diagram and the signed velocity-time graph. Questions now include maximum-height calculation and positive/negative graph-area processing.

excluded_mapped_parts.9702_s16_21_q02_c: Its horizontal-component and resultant-displacement demand belongs to projectile motion, so it is not directly assessed in Lesson 10.

blocks.title: Zero velocity, but not zero acceleration
body: Throw a soft ball straight upward. At the highest point it pauses for an instant. Is gravity also paused at that instant? Predict before reading on.
The velocity is zero for one instant, but gravity is still acting. The acceleration remains 9.81 m s^-2 downward. That difference between velocity and acceleration unlocks the whole journey.

figure.purpose: Expose the zero-velocity versus non-zero-acceleration puzzle.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn three-frame ball sequence rising, at the top, and beginning to fall, with velocity arrows changing and equal downward acceleration arrows.
figure.alt_text: A ball rising, momentarily at rest at its highest point, and falling, while downward acceleration is present in all three frames.

blocks.title: One acceleration through the turn
body: Choose upward as positive. During ascent, u is positive and a = -9.81 m s^-2. The negative acceleration reduces the positive velocity until v = 0.
After the top, velocity becomes negative because the ball moves downward. Acceleration stays negative. Velocity changes sign at the turn, but acceleration does not.

figure.purpose: Show which signed quantities change at maximum height.
figure.brief: Teacher-sketch sign table for ascent, top and descent using upward positive, showing v positive, zero and negative while a remains negative.
figure.alt_text: A sign table across ascent, maximum height and descent with acceleration negative throughout.

blocks.title: Find the top without guessing
body: Formula to remember: v = u + at. Here u and v are velocities in m s^-1, a is acceleration in m s^-2 and t is time in s. At the top, set v = 0 to find ascent time.
Formula to remember: v^2 = u^2 + 2as. Here s is displacement in m. At the top, v = 0, so this route finds maximum height without time.
Formula to remember: s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2. This can track displacement at any time while acceleration is constant.

figure.purpose: Connect the turning-point condition to two equation routes.
figure.brief: Branching worked-layout sketch from v = 0 at the top to a time route and a height route.
figure.alt_text: The condition v equals zero at maximum height branching to equations for ascent time and maximum height.

blocks.title: A ball launched upward
body: A ball leaves a hand at +14.0 m s^-1. Take upward as positive, so a = -9.81 m s^-2.
For ascent time, use 0 = 14.0 - 9.81t. This gives t = 1.43 s.
For maximum height above the hand, use 0 = 14.0^2 + 2(-9.81)s. This gives s = 9.99 m.
If it returns to the hand and air resistance is negligible, the descent from the top mirrors the ascent in time. This symmetry applies only when start and finish heights match.

figure.purpose: Model stage boundaries and valid symmetry conditions.
figure.brief: Annotated vertical route from hand to top and back to hand with ascent and descent stages, equal-height endpoints and no answer-revealing labels beyond given launch speed.
figure.alt_text: A ball travels from a hand to a highest point and returns to the same hand height, divided into ascent and descent stages.

blocks.title: Measure g with a falling object
body: Hold a small dense ball with an electromagnet above a trapdoor or impact switch. Measure the vertical distance s from the bottom of the ball at release to the contact point. Release the ball and use electronic timing so the timer starts at release and stops at impact.

For release from rest, s = \frac{1}{2}gt^2. Repeat at each distance and average the time. Use several distances. Plot s on the vertical axis against t^2 on the horizontal axis. The gradient is g/2, so g = 2 times the gradient.

A single short fall makes reaction or switching delays a large fraction of the time. Electronic release, a common start signal, larger suitable distances and repeated readings reduce this problem. Measure from consistent reference points and keep the fall vertical.

figure.purpose: Make apparatus, measured distance and timing triggers unambiguous.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn apparatus with electromagnet, dense ball, metre rule, impact switch and timer wires, with distance endpoints marked.
figure.alt_text: A falling-ball setup using an electromagnet, metre rule, impact switch and electronic timer.

blocks.title: Why the graph gives g
body: The equation s = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 has the form y = mx. If y is s and x is t^2, the graph should be a straight line through the origin with gradient g/2.

Using many points is stronger than calculating g from one fall. A best-fit line reduces the influence of random timing variation. A non-zero intercept can warn of a fixed timing delay or a distance reference error.

figure.purpose: Link the physical equation to graph axes and gradient processing.
figure.brief: Teacher-sketch s against t squared graph with best-fit line, gradient triangle and label g = 2 times gradient, plus a small non-zero-intercept caution inset.
figure.alt_text: A straight-line graph of distance against time squared with a gradient triangle used to determine g.

blocks.title: Complete flight from a balcony
body: A ball is launched upward at 14.0 m s^-1 from a balcony 6.0 m above the ground. Take upward as positive, so a = -9.81 m s^-2.
Ascent: at the turning point v = 0. From v = u + at, t_up = (0 - 14.0)/(-9.81) = 1.43 s.
The rise is found from v^2 = u^2 + 2as: 0 = 14.0^2 + 2(-9.81)s, so s = 9.99 m. The top is 16.0 m above ground.
Whole flight: ground is s = -6.0 m from launch. Use -6.0 = 14.0t - 4.905t^2. The positive root gives t = 3.24 s.
Impact: v = 14.0 + (-9.81)(3.24) = -17.8 m s^-1. The minus sign means downward. Check using v^2 = 14.0^2 + 2(-9.81)(-6.0), which gives speed 17.7 m s^-1.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in complete flight from a balcony visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for complete flight from a balcony.

blocks.title: From measurements to g
body: Drop a small dense ball from rest and measure several pairs of fall distance s and time t using light gates or video frames.
For a release from rest, s = 1/2 gt^2. Plot s on the vertical axis against t^2 on the horizontal axis.
A best-fit straight line has gradient g/2, so g = 2 x gradient. Repeating distances reduces the effect of one timing error.
A non-zero intercept suggests a timing or release offset. A scatter of points suggests random uncertainty.
Independent route: calculate 2s/t^2 for each run and compare the mean with twice the graph gradient. Agreement supports the processing.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in from measurements to g visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for from measurements to g.

blocks.title: One model, two uses
body: For upward motion, keep downward g throughout and use v = 0 only as the turning-point condition. Split the journey when the question needs separate ascent and descent stages.

For the experiment, release from rest, measure s and t electronically, repeat across several distances, plot s against t^2 and double the gradient. The opening pause never meant gravity stopped. It marked the instant when velocity changed sign under the same downward acceleration.

concepts_taught: At maximum height, velocity is zero but acceleration remains downward g.
Upward launch has ascent and descent stages joined at a turning point.
A falling-object experiment can determine g from s = 1/2 gt^2.
A graph of s against t^2 has gradient g/2.
misconceptions_addressed: Zero velocity at maximum height means zero acceleration.
One fall time is enough for a reliable g measurement.
The gradient of s against t squared equals g.
skills_students_can_now_use: Calculate ascent time and maximum height.
Describe a falling-object experiment for g.
Process repeated data using an s against t squared graph and evaluate limitations.
next_lesson_can_assume: Students can analyse complete one-dimensional vertical motion under constant g.
Students distinguish zero velocity from zero acceleration.
Students can obtain g from a falling-object experiment and graph.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Students can separate horizontal and vertical projectile components.
Students know projectile paths or range calculations.
Students can recombine perpendicular velocity components.
